conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this hospital stay. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m okay. A little anxious. This is my third chemo cycle, right? I just want to get through it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re doing great so far. We’re here to make sure everything goes smoothly. We’ll start with some labs and get you ready for your methotrexate tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My foot’s still hurting—same as last time. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re watching that closely. Last time, the ultrasound and MRI didn’t show a blood clot or nerve compression. We think it’s related to either your MS or the chemo. We’ll keep you on gabapentin and adjust it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lip—I’ve got this sore on the right side. It’s new. Could that be a cold sore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a herpes simplex lesion. Since you’re on steroids, which can weaken your immune response, we’re going to start you on acyclovir to prevent it from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had cold sores before, but not during chemo. Is that common?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen, especially with steroids. That’s why we’re being proactive. The acyclovir will help keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my liver numbers were high last time. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. The transaminitis is likely due to the methotrexate. Your hepatitis tests came back negative, so it’s not an infection. We’ll keep an eye on it and support your liver with hydration and bicarbonate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’m still on the blood thinner for the clot from last cycle?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, enoxaparin twice a day. We’re continuing that to prevent another clot. You’re also getting it as extra protection during this hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything we can to prevent that. Now, tomorrow morning, you’ll have a port placed before chemo. It’ll make the infusion easier and safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the procedure in my neck? I saw it on the schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small catheter will be placed in your right internal jugular vein, with the port under the skin on your chest. It’s done with ultrasound and X-ray guidance. Very safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation and local numbing. Most patients feel pressure but not pain. Afterward, you might have some soreness, but we’ll manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And the chemo—same dose as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, high-dose methotrexate at 8 grams per square meter. We’ll give you IV bicarbonate before and during to protect your kidneys and help clear the drug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We start it 24 hours after chemo and give it every six hours to rescue your healthy cells. We’ll check your methotrexate levels daily to guide how long you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Ready for your port placement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: As ready as I’ll ever be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port was placed successfully. The tip is in the right spot, and it’s ready to use. You did great. Any discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little sore where they put it. Nothing bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on it. Now, we’ll start your methotrexate infusion this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your chemo now. We’ve given IV bicarbonate to alkalinize your urine. This helps the methotrexate leave your body safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will the infusion take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About four hours. You’ll stay hydrated with IV fluids containing bicarbonate. We’ll check your urine pH regularly to make sure it stays above 7.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infusion is complete. You tolerated it well. No nausea or reactions. We’ll start leucovorin tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My foot’s aching more today. Can we do anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can increase your gabapentin from 300 mg twice a day to 400 mg three times a day. We’ll also keep oxycodone available for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, let’s try that. And my lip sore—is the acyclovir helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should reduce healing time and prevent new outbreaks. Keep it clean and let us know if it worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your methotrexate level this morning is 0.44, which is low and expected. We’ll continue leucovorin every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Last time I had to stay longer because of high levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This level is actually good. It means the drug is clearing well. You won’t need extra leucovorin or bicarbonate beyond what we’re already giving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about my liver tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ALT and AST are still elevated but coming down—from 199 to 155 and 112 to 60. This suggests improvement. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a lumbar puncture tomorrow to check your spinal fluid for any lymphoma cells. It’s a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt? I’ve never had one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get numbing medicine. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It takes about 20 minutes. We do it to make sure the lymphoma hasn’t spread to the spinal fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it has?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d treat it with intrathecal chemotherapy. But based on your symptoms and scans, it’s unlikely. This is just being thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lumbar puncture went well. You did great. The fluid will be tested, but results will take a few days. For now, we’re discharging you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? I feel okay. But what about the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you with the results. You’re stable, your methotrexate is cleared, and your pain is managed. You’ll follow up with oncology in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Gabapentin is now 400 mg three times a day for your foot pain. And you’ll stay on acyclovir three times a day until your steroids are stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And enoxaparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day. Continue that exactly as prescribed. Any questions before we wrap up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think that’s everything. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you soon. Take care and call if anything changes.
